title: How Guerrilla Gardening Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain guerrilla gardening: covertly planting or tending neglected public or vacant land. They open with Josh's anecdote about a friend's firefighter father and "clumping" (stealing plants from neighbors' yards). They cover the history, starting with Gerard Winston Lee and the Diggers in England in 1969, then Liz Christie and the Green Guerrillas in New York in the early 1970s, including the Bowery site that became a memorial park. They discuss seed bombs (clay, compost and seed balls, with a link to Richard Reynolds). They describe Reynolds' London work and his apartment-complex garden dispute, a police encounter caught on video, and a Boulder, Colorado case in which a man was reportedly threatened with a fine for planting vegetables in a street strip. They also cover the political side of the practice, tips for starting (pick neglected strips, use native non-invasive plants, drought-resistant plants that need little upkeep, work at night or in daytime), and a listener mail about turkey vultures.

segments.title: Opening banter and clumping anecdote
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show. Josh recounts a childhood friend's firefighter father and his friends who 'clumped' by stealing plants from neighbors' yards, which leads into a segue to guerrilla gardening.

segments.title: What guerrilla gardening is
segments.summary: Defined as stealth planting and tending of untended, neglected, or overgrown vacant lots. The hosts say it is subversive but harmless and can improve a neighborhood, though some people try to shut it down.

segments.title: History: The Diggers and the Green Guerrillas
segments.summary: Gerard Winston Lee started the Diggers in England in 1969 and they planted vegetables on land they did not own. The modern version began in New York in the early 1970s, when Liz Christie founded the Green Guerrillas. Their first site was at the corner of the Bowery, which later became a memorial park dedicated to Christie after a struggle with the city.

segments.title: Seed bombs
segments.summary: Christie first used condoms filled with seeds and compost, which the hosts say did not work well. Modern seed bombs are clay, compost, and seed balls that are dried and thrown, often before rain, and can be tossed from a car.

segments.title: Richard Reynolds and London disputes
segments.summary: Richard Reynolds, founder of the London guerrilla gardening movement, ran a website and a how-to video on seed bombs. At his apartment complex, residents disputed paying for maintenance, he was refunded, and later an agreement with management broke down. A police encounter in London over a street-corner garden was caught on video.

segments.title: Rules, enforcement, and protest
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how rule-following neighbors and code enforcement can turn guerrilla gardening into a crime. They describe its political side as protest against urban blight and rising food costs, and the Boulder, Colorado case in which Scott Hoffenburg was reportedly threatened with a large fine for planting vegetables in a street strip.

segments.title: How to get started
segments.summary: Tips for beginners: find neglected spots such as street-sidewalk strips and corners, choose indigenous non-invasive plants (kudzu is cited as a warning), pick drought-resistant, low-upkeep plants, get donations or buy plants, and work alone or with a team, often at night.

segments.title: Further resources
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to Richard Reynolds' website and book, and to the HowStuffWorks article on the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: turkey vulture
segments.summary: Listener Leah Johnson writes about being puked on by a turkey vulture while volunteering in a raptor rehabilitation program. The hosts send her steak knives.
